forms.desc: Persian writes numbers with the Indo-Persian digits `۰ ۱ ۲ ۳ ۴ ۵ ۶ ۷ ۸ ۹`
each digit's pronunciation is introduced at first appearance in this chapter. Teens 11–19 are unique single words (`یازده` _yāzdah_ "11", not "one-one")

forms.note: multiples of ten (20, 30 …) are likewise independent words. Verse numbers count as first occurrences, so each verse opens with its numeral's entry

entries.title: Grammar: Possessive / pronominal suffixes
entries.body: Persian attaches possessive clitics directly to nouns: _-am_ (my), _-at_ (thy), _-aš_ (his/her/its), _-mān_ (our), _-tān_ (your), _-šān_ (their). These are preferred over the longer `[noun] + [full pronoun]` construction.

examples.persian: خانواده اش
examples.en: his family

examples.persian: پدرشان
examples.en: their father

entries.closing: The clitic attaches after the full noun phrase: `برادرانش` = "his brothers", `پسرانش` = "his sons", `پدرم` = "my father."

entries.meaning: 3sg possessive clitic ("his/her/its"), written with a space in the publisher's edition

forms.desc: other persons: `ام` _-am_ (1sg), `ات` _-at_ (2sg), `مان` _-mān_ (1pl), `تان` _-tān_ (2pl), `شان` _-šān_ (3pl). In perfect constructions `ام` is also the 1sg copula clitic: `کرده ام` "I have done."

entries.title: Grammar: Direct-object marker `را`
entries.body: `را` marks a **specific or definite** direct object. It attaches to the end of the entire object phrase — after relative clauses, adjectives, or possessive-suffixed nouns.

examples.persian: آنها دارایی{e} خود را باقی می گذارند
examples.en: They leave their own possessions behind. [`را` follows the whole phrase `دارایی خود`]

examples.persian: خانه اش را ترک کرد
examples.en: He left his house. [`را` follows the possessive-suffixed noun]

entries.title: Grammar: Ezafe chains
entries.body: The unstressed suffix _-e_ (spelled as a kasra ِ on consonant-final words, or as ی on ā/ū-final words) links a head noun to its modifiers: **head – modifier – modifier – …**

examples.persian: بیابانِ کنار{e} دریای سرخ
examples.en: the wilderness beside the Red Sea [three-link chain: wilderness ← beside ← sea-of-red]

entries.closing: The publisher rarely writes the kasra; this guide marks every editorial ezafe with `{e}` in accent-color so you can distinguish added from original.

entries.title: Grammar: Imperfective `می-` and its negation `نمی-`
entries.body: The prefix _mī-_ marks non-perfective aspect. Added to the present stem + endings → **present tense** ("he takes"). Added to the past stem + endings → **past habitual / continuous** ("he was taking / used to take"). Negation fuses: `نمی‌بَرد` "he does not take." In compound verbs `می-` attaches only to the light verb: `نیایش می‌کند` "prays", `باقی می‌گذارند` "they leave behind."

examples.persian: لیحای خانواده اش را … می بَرد
examples.en: Lehi takes his family …

the unmarked `سرور` is the citation form used here. Vocative `سرورا` _Sarvarā_ "O Lord!" [verse 19](#verse-19)

entries.title: Grammar: Archaic / biblical register
entries.body:
The translator deliberately chose high-register Persian to mirror the KJV-style English of the original. Key markers:

- `گفتا` (_goftā_) — archaic narrative past of `گفتن`, roughly "said he" (the `-ā` is a classical Persian narrative suffix).
- `آری` (_ārī_) — "yea, indeed"; literary equivalent of `بله`.
- `بنگرید` (_benegarīd_) — "behold!" (2pl imperative of `نگریستن`).
- `سرور` (_Sarvar_) — "master, chief" repurposed as "the Lord." Vocative `سرورا` [verse 19](#verse-19) uses the classical `-ā` ending.
- Bookish verbs over everyday equivalents: `آموختن` (not `یاد دادن`) for "to teach"; `نیایش کردن` (not `دعا کردن`) for "to pray."

examples.persian: سخن گفت، گفتا: ای کاش تو هم می توانستی مانند این رودخانه باشی
examples.translit: soxan goft, goftā: ey kāš to ham mī-tavānestī mānand-e īn rūdxāne bāšī
examples.en: he spoke, saying: O that thou couldest be like unto this river.

entries.title: Grammar: Compound verbs (light-verb constructions)
entries.body: Persian builds most of its verbs as **[noun or adjective] + [light verb]**. The meaning lives in the first element; the light verb (most often `کردن`, `شدن`, `دادن`, `گذاشتن`) handles inflection. In formal/literary Persian, compound-verb subjunctives **drop the `بـ-` prefix**: `نگه دارند` (not `*نگه بدارند`), `فرمانروایی کند` (not `*فرمانروایی بکند`).

examples.persian: با ایمان نیایش می کند
examples.en: prays with faith [`نیایش کردن` = to pray]

entries.closing: Examples from this chapter: `نیایش کردن` (to pray), `غرولند کردن` (to murmur), `سپاسگزاری کردن` (to give thanks), `ترک کردن` (to leave/abandon), `باور کردن` (to believe), `زاری کردن` (to implore), `دیدار کردن` (to appear to/visit), `فرمانروایی کردن` (to reign).

entries.title: Grammar: Passive voice with `شدن`
entries.body: Persian forms the passive analytically: **[past participle] + شدن** (conjugated). The agent, if named, uses `از سوی` ("by the hand of") or `توسط`.

examples.persian: او برگزیده می شود

entries.title: Grammar: `چنین گذشت که` — "And it came to pass that"
entries.body:
The most frequent syntactic frame in the Persian Book of Mormon. Literally "thus it passed that," it mirrors the Hebrew/English _wayyiqtol_ narrative formula. The main clause verb is always in the past tense.

Structure: `چنین گذشت که` + [narrative clause in past].

examples.persian: چنین گذشت که سرور بر پدرم سخن گفت
examples.translit: čonīn gozašt ke Sarvar bar pedar-am soxan goft
examples.en: It came to pass that the Lord spake unto my father.

examples.persian: چنین گذشت که هنگامی که او سه روز مسافرت کرد
examples.translit: čonīn gozašt ke hangāmī ke ū se rūz mosāferat kard
examples.en: It came to pass that when he had traveled three days…

entries.closing: This frame opens eleven of twenty-four verses in this chapter.

entries.title: Grammar: Resultative perfect — `برکت یافته هستی`
entries.body: **[past participle] + [copula]** expresses a _resultant state_: the action is complete and its outcome still holds.

examples.persian: برکت یافته هستی تو لیحای
examples.en: Blessed art thou, Lehi. [literally: "you are in a state of having found blessing"]

entries.closing: Compare `یافت` (simple past: "he received") with `یافته هستی` (resultative: "thou art in possession of having received"). The biblical translation reserves this construction for divine declarations and elevated speech.

entries.title: Grammar: Relative clause with `که`
entries.body: `که` relativizes nouns of any semantic role. The relative head in the main clause often takes the indefinite suffix `-ی` (or `-یی`) as a correlative marker; the relative verb is in the indicative or past perfect.

examples.persian: چیزهایی را که من به تو فرمان دادم
examples.translit: čīzhāyī-rā ke man be to farmān dādam
examples.en: the things that I commanded thee [head `چیزهایی` + acc. `را` + rel. clause]

examples.persian: کارهائی که تو انجام داده ای
examples.en: the things thou hast done [past perfect: pp. `داده` + 2sg copula `ای`]

entries.closing: The past perfect `[pp.] + [copula ای/است/بودی…]` expresses an action completed before the narrative present.

forms.desc: with imperfective `می`: `می بایستی` _mī-bāyestī_ / `می بایست` _mī-bāyest_ "was to, should (past obligation)." Impersonal — used for all persons

entries.title: Grammar: `می بایستی` — past modal obligation
entries.body: `باید` is a **defective impersonal verb** meaning "it is necessary, must, should." Its past imperfect form `می بایستی` expresses an obligation or necessity in reported or past context.

examples.persian: که او می بایستی خانواده اش را بردارد
examples.en: that he should take his family [past modal + subjunctive complement]

entries.closing: The dependent verb `بردارد` is in the **subjunctive** (bare stem, `بـ-` dropped in formal/literary style). Compare the present: `باید بردارد` "he must take."

entries.title: Grammar: `ای کاش` + imperfect — wishing construction
entries.body: `ای کاش` (also written `ای کاشکی`) introduces an unfulfilled or unlikely wish: "O that …, would that …, if only …." The verb in the wish clause takes the **past imperfect** (می + past stem), not the subjunctive — a crucial distinction from purpose clauses.

examples.persian: ای کاش تو هم می توانستی مانند این رودخانه باشی پیوسته روانه
examples.translit: ey kāš to ham mī-tavānestī mānand-e īn rūdxāne bāšī pīvaste ravāne
examples.en: O that thou mightest be like unto this river, continually running. [past impf. `می توانستی` + subjunctive complement `باشی`]

examples.persian: ای کاش تو هم می توانستی مانند این وادی باشی، پایدار و استوار

examples.en: O that thou mightest be like unto this valley, firm and steadfast.

entries.closing: The `ای` is a vocative/expressive particle; `کاش` is the wish particle (related to Arabic _kāšku_). Together they form a fixed phrase. The embedded subjunctive `باشی` follows the modal complement `توانستی`.

entries.body: `تا جایی که` (lit. "to the place/extent that") introduces a condition whose apodosis (result clause) takes the future `خواه-` + infinitive. The conditional verb is in the **present subjunctive**.

intro:
## Intro
Chapter 2 of 1 Nephi follows directly from chapter 1: Lehi has received a dream in which the Lord warned him that the Jews seek his life, and he is now commanded to take his family and flee into the wilderness. In twenty-four verses the narrative moves through five episodes: the family's departure from Jerusalem southward to the Red Sea (vv. 1–6); Lehi's erection of a stone altar and sacrifice of thanksgiving (v. 7); his impassioned wish that Laman and Lemuel would be as faithful as the river and as constant as the valley (vv. 8–10); their murmuring explained and contrasted with young Nephi's prayer (vv. 11–18); and a personal revelation to Nephi that commissions him as future ruler and teacher — or warns that the brothers will become a scourge if they persist in rebellion (vv. 19–24).
Vocabulary spans six domains: **journey / wilderness** (بیابان، دریای سرخ، وادی، رود), **possessions / leaving** (دارایی، طلا، نقره، چادر), **sacrifice / worship** (قربانگاه، قربانی، پیشکش، سپاسگزاری), **commandment / obedience** (فرمان، مطیع، نگه داشتن), **murmuring / stubbornness** (غرولند، خیره سری، سخت دلی), and **revelation / promise** (نیایش، ایمان، برگزیدن، فرمانروایی). Grammar highlights unique to this chapter include the wishing construction _ای کاش + imperfect_ (vv. 9–10) and the conditional _تا جایی که + subjunctive_ (vv. 20–22).
vocab_intro: Organized in **order of first appearance**, grouped by the chapter summary and then verse-by-verse. Every distinct lemma in the chapter is introduced at its first occurrence — including all function words. Inflected forms of a verb already introduced are not re-listed as fresh entries; they are handled by the _Forms_ sub-bullet on the original entry. Proper nouns are listed where they first appear, tagged `[proper]`. Verbs include the infinitive and present stem.
closing: Chapter 2 is built on two opposing grammatical registers. The narrative framework — `چنین گذشت که` opening eleven verses — trains the reader to scan for that phrase as a scene-marker; once recognized, parsing the clause that follows becomes automatic. Within that frame, two constructions do the theological work: `ای کاش + imperfect` (vv. 9–10), which casts Lehi's wish for his sons as explicitly unfulfilled, and `تا جایی که + subjunctive / future` (vv. 20–22), which frames Nephi's commission as conditional rather than absolute. Mastering these three patterns — the narrative frame, the unfulfilled wish, and the conditional promise — gives you the skeleton of almost every scene in the book. As a study habit, read each `چنین گذشت که` clause and identify the verb in the trailing clause before moving to the vocabulary; that single step will double your reading speed across 1 Nephi.
